analysis.one_liner: Ends the exemption that lets 55-and-older housing communities exclude families with children.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2024 with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Housing Act bars housing discrimination against families with children, but a 1988 carve-out known as the Thurmond amendment lets communities restricted to residents 55 and older turn families with children away. This one-page bill strikes that carve-out from the law. It never moved past the referral stage.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children who are turned away from age-restricted housing, and housing seekers generally, because age restrictions on housing stock would no longer be lawful. Fair-housing enforcement groups would gain a broader rule to apply.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends section 807(b) of the Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. 3607(b)) by striking paragraph (4), the provision commonly called the Thurmond amendment, and renumbering the remaining paragraphs [S2].

Paragraph (4) is the statutory exemption that allows 'housing for older persons' — communities restricted to residents 55 and over or 62 and over — to operate outside the Act's ban on familial-status discrimination [S2]. Removing it would make age-restricted communities subject to the same nondiscrimination rules as everyone else [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Operators and developers of 55+ communities, whose entire business model rests on excluding families with children, and residents of those communities, who chose them for the child-free environment and would lose the legal guarantee of it.

drawbacks.text: Older residents who deliberately chose age-restricted communities — and paid premiums for them — would lose the legal assurance that children cannot move in next door, and communities could no longer market themselves that way [S2].

Striking the exemption would force existing 55+ communities to restructure their rules, admission policies, and marketing, and would put the federal government in the position of second-guessing a housing arrangement Congress deliberately created in 1988 and has preserved since.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families shut out of age-restricted housing, the bill removes a real legal barrier. But the carve-out it repeals is not a loophole in any ordinary sense — it is a deliberate, decades-old policy choice that lets older Americans live in communities built around their stage of life, and many residents would experience its repeal as taking something away from them. The bill, a single provision introduced in the final weeks of the session, made no attempt to phase in or soften that change, and it drew no cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on September 19, 2024, read twice, and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Booker introduced the Fair Future Act in the Senate on September 19, 2024 [S4].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S4].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing carve-out stands, so 55+ housing operators keep their legal ability to exclude families with children and their residents keep the age-restricted guarantee. Families with children who want that housing are no better off than before.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; sole sponsor

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no recorded votes or public positions, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Age-restricted (55+) housing developers and community operators
industries.note: Their product depends on the legal right to exclude families with children; repealing the Thurmond amendment would erase that right and force a rewrite of their communities' rules and marketing [S2]. From the operator's standpoint, that interest runs against families seeking housing.
Not an industry but a concentrated interest: older homeowners and renters who paid for age-restricted living would lose the guarantee their community stays child-free [S2].
